Deco Symmetry 4

TrianglesGeometryArea
Game: A triangle and its upside-down mirror can be built from the very same three pieces; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the top dot or slide the two base dots. Tick the boxes to show names or right-angle marks, then press Move them to see the pieces turn.

Keyboard: Tab to a dot, then use the arrow keys (Shift makes a bigger step).

Look for the math

Here is a triangle with a flat base. Its mirror image sits the other way up. The book's solution to the old puzzle uses only two cuts — and not one piece needs to be turned over. This applet gives a new way to see why it works, rather than a new dissection.

The mirror between two lines

B and C slide along one horizontal line while A moves freely. The mirror is a reflection in the horizontal line halfway between A and the base: A' has A's x and the base's y, while B' and C' have the base points' x and A's y. So A' lands on the base whenever A stands above the segment BC. If A moves out to one side, the cut fails and the applet switches "Move them" off. Earlier applets in this series used a vertical mirror line and different pieces (three for acute triangles, four in general, or three kites from the incenter); this fourth one uses the horizontal midline and just three pieces for every valid position.

Two cuts, two half turns

Let D be where AB crosses A'B', and E where AC crosses A'C'. Because the base is flat, D is the midpoint of both AB and A'B', and E is the midpoint of both AC and A'C'. The two cuts A'D and A'E split the triangle into three pieces. A half turn about D sends A' to B' and B to A; a half turn about E sends A' to C' and C to A. The middle piece A'DAE already fits both triangles. Every move is a turn, never a flip, so this is a direct equidecomposition. The logic test checked 4,655 valid layouts: the pieces fill both triangles, their side lengths match, and their orientation keeps its sign.

Four isosceles triangles

A'D and A'E are perpendicular bisectors of A'B and A'C, so the two end pieces are isosceles. The middle four-sided piece is split by the line AA': D and E lie on the middle line between A and A', so those two halves are isosceles too. That gives four isosceles triangles; the test found no exception in 4,655 valid layouts nor in 500 arbitrary triangles turned so one of their sides became the base.

The shorter decompositions

The page also notes two special cases. For an acute triangle, join the circumcenter to the three corners: it lies inside, and its equal distances to the corners give three isosceles triangles. For a right triangle, join the right corner to the midpoint of the hypotenuse: that midpoint is equally far from all three corners, giving two isosceles triangles. Both claims were checked over a grid of triangles.

Try sliding A to the left edge of the base: the two cuts switch off, because A' is no longer on the base. Then bring A back and press "Move them".
